conflicts: Clarity proposes: Enlarge the board substantially and pull the controls and objectives closer to its left and right edges, creating one compact gameplay group rather than three distant islands. That prioritization is valid only if every requested object, state, and relationship remains visibly substantive; reducing or demoting required content would trade compliance for neatness. Visual System & Craft proposes: Trim the board container precisely to the 10-column grid and establish one tile-gap, border, and inset-shadow token. System consolidation must not homogenize semantically required elements until their roles become merely decorative. Expressiveness proposes: Give player, crates, lever, door, and targets distinct foundry-specific silhouettes and state changes, introduce purposeful floor wear and heat markings along likely routes, and create one expressive lever-to-door visual linkage while preserving board readability. The expressive addition is acceptable only when it strengthens the requested experience rather than replacing required content or interaction evidence.
accept: Accept Clarity's grouping and label-to-object improvements because they make required relationships visibly legible. Accept Craft's cleanup of construction, typography, and state consistency wherever it preserves all required elements. Accept Expressiveness's content-specific imagery and differentiation when it makes the intended game or scene more immediately recognizable.
compromise: Start with the fidelity-critical action: Preserve the complete board, player, two crates, two goals, controls, HUD, and objectives, but make the mechanic relationships explicit. Then adopt the other reviewers' hierarchy, token, and expressive refinements within that preserved requirement map. No requested element may be deleted, cropped, reduced to a label, or visually subordinated below its intended role; simplify presentation and unify styling around the complete artifact instead.
